channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: Human Routers of Machine Words
item.description: This article explores the concept of individuals acting as 'human routers' for AI, effectively using artificial intelligence as a cognitive extension to organize and process complex thoughts. It highlights how humans integrate machine-generated text into their own intellectual workflows to enhance reasoning and output.

item.title: Reading List 06/13/2026
item.description: This reading list explores diverse engineering and infrastructure topics, ranging from architectural integration of housing and libraries to heavy manufacturing and large-scale geopolitical infrastructure projects. It highlights unique developments in construction, defense, and international transport concepts.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 13 June 2026
item.description: This weekly digest covers key security updates in package management, including npm v12 breaking changes regarding lifecycle scripts and remote dependencies. It also highlights new features in uv for vulnerability auditing and malware detection, as well as pnpm's hardened bootstrapping process.

item.title: RSA munitions T-shirt
item.description: The article recounts the historical protest by Adam Back in 1995, who printed an obfuscated RSA encryption algorithm on T-shirts to challenge US export restrictions on cryptography. This act highlighted the absurd government classification of code as munitions during the period of strict encryption regulation.

item.title: Dangerous Technology For Americans Only
item.description: The article critiques the US government's export control directives on AI models, noting how Anthropic's 'safety' framing has resulted in restrictions based on nationality rather than objective risk. The author argues that treating AI as a weapon for exclusive American use promotes nationalism and division, serving as a warning to non-US citizens about the geopolitical shift in technology control.

item.title: The adder at the heart of Intel's 8087 floating-point chip
item.description: This article explores the technical design of the 69-bit adder within the Intel 8087 floating-point coprocessor. It details how the chip uses specific architectural innovations to handle complex arithmetic and carry operations efficiently.

item.title: Pluralistic: Shareholder supremacy and the precog CEO (13 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques Milton Friedman's 55-year-old doctrine of shareholder supremacy, which mandates that corporate managers focus exclusively on profit maximization. The article argues that this theory, intended to provide an objective metric for business success, is essentially unfalsifiable and flawed in its premise.

item.title: Statement on the US government directive to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5
item.description: Anthropic has been directed by the US government to suspend access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models due to alleged national security risks related to jailbreaking. The company contests the severity of these concerns, noting that the reported capabilities are already widely available in other models used for security research.

item.title: OpenAI WebRTC Audio Session, now with document context
item.description: Simon Willison has updated his WebRTC audio tool to support OpenAI's latest GPT-Realtime-2 model. Users can now input custom document context to engage in real-time, voice-based conversations about specific textual information directly within their browser.

item.title: I Am Not a Reverse Centaur
item.description: The author discusses the increasing influx of LLM-generated pull requests in open-source projects, which threatens to turn experienced maintainers into 'reverse centaurs'—humans who spend their time reviewing machine-made code. He reaffirms his refusal to rely on LLMs and outlines his approach to maintaining personal agency while managing these contributions.

item.title: This Week on The Analog Antiquarian
item.description: This entry from The Digital Antiquarian explores the early game development history surrounding the title Henry VI, Part 1. It examines the technical and creative context of this specific software release within the broader timeline of early computing history.

item.title: AI will be massively deflationary
item.description: The article argues that anxieties surrounding AI companies like Anthropic are overstated, suggesting that the underlying technology is becoming a commodity. It posits that while these firms may hold grand ideologies, the competitive nature of the industry and economic realities will lead to deflationary effects rather than total control.

item.title: Joint Guidance on Vulnerability Naming and Disclosure
item.description: The Vulnerability Naming Authority has established a standardized, unified process for naming and disclosing vulnerabilities in the United States. This framework introduces centralized registry requirements, including specific branding elements like logos and color palettes, alongside a deconfliction database to ensure unique naming.

item.title: Understanding the rationale behind a rule when trying to circumvent it
item.description: This post reflects on the nuances of following rules versus attempting to circumvent them. It highlights the importance of understanding the underlying rationale of a rule rather than just adhering to its literal technicality.

item.title: Why are cached input tokens cheaper with AI services?
item.description: This article explains why AI services offer lower costs for cached input tokens. It highlights that caching reduces the computational burden on GPUs, as they do not need to perform redundant calculations for previously processed sequences.

item.title: Gadget Review: TP Link EH210 Ethernet Splitter (USB-C) ★★★★★
item.description: This post reviews the TP Link EH210, a compact USB-C Ethernet splitter designed for rooms with limited device requirements. The author evaluates its practical application for simplifying home networking in spaces that do not necessitate a full-sized Ethernet switch.

item.title: Pluralistic: Google's new remote attestation scheme is every bit as terrible as its old remote attestation scheme (12 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques Google's remote attestation schemes, arguing they undermine the fundamental role of browsers as user agents. He emphasizes that browsers must remain interoperable and obedient to the user rather than enforcing manufacturer-dictated restrictions.

item.title: I can never fully embrace LLMs for code
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author reflects on the conflict between the convenience of AI-generated code and the necessity of understanding it. Unlike using established libraries, AI outputs lack vetting and consistency, leading the author to prioritize code comprehension over the speed gains offered by LLMs.

item.title: Quoting Andrew Singleton
item.description: This post features a satirical excerpt from Andrew Singleton's 'AI Economics for Dummies' that critiques the circular and inflated nature of current AI investment models. The piece uses a metaphorical story about a crematorium to highlight the lack of genuine financial substance behind some high-profile AI revenue claims.

item.title: Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive
item.description: Simon Willison shares his experience with the proactive capabilities of Claude Fable 5, specifically in debugging software. He illustrates how the AI independently explores local project dependencies and files to troubleshoot UI glitches based on a simple screenshot and prompt.

item.title: You can finally power on a Mac remotely
item.description: Apple has introduced a new feature allowing users to power on Mac computers remotely, addressing long-standing usability issues. While media reports link this to the controversial M4 Mac mini power button placement, the author highlights its broader utility for server and remote access management.

item.title: Hacking Google with A.I. for $500,000
item.description: The author shares the findings of an extensive security audit conducted by deploying AI to analyze Google's vast infrastructure. The project resulted in identifying numerous vulnerabilities across 1,500 APIs and 3,600 keys, earning the researcher $500,000 in bug bounties.

item.title: My Portable Heater
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The author explores the Gigabyte Aorus RTX 5060 Ti AI Box, an external GPU that bridges the gap between portability and performance. While initially dismissed by gamers for desktop use, its compact design and increased RAM make it a compelling tool for laptop users and AI enthusiasts.

item.title: Biological Evolution and Information Acquisition
item.description: This post discusses a simulation by economist Brian Arthur that models technological evolution. It demonstrates how complex systems can emerge from simple building blocks through the iterative combination of functional components.

item.title: What Happened to tea.xyz
item.description: The article analyzes the decline of tea.xyz, a cryptocurrency project aimed at rewarding open-source maintainers that lost 90% of its value shortly after launch. It examines the project's background, its split into the pkgx package manager and the tea crypto protocol, and the flaws in its Proof of Contribution incentive model.

item.title: Solving a chess puzzle with Claude and Prolog
item.description: This article explores the use of Prolog, a logic programming language, for solving chess puzzles. It discusses the linguistic origins of Prolog and highlights its unique ability to represent logical problems directly while weighing its pros and cons.

item.title: Formally proving a calculation with Claude and Lean
item.description: This post details an experiment using the AI model Claude to generate Lean code for verifying a specific mathematical proof involving Fourier coefficients and Bessel functions. The author explores the potential for large language models to assist in formal mathematical verification.

item.title: What’s the opposite of Clip­Cursor that lets me exclude the cursor from a region?
item.description: The article addresses whether Windows offers a built-in feature to exclude the cursor from a specific region, similar to how ClipCursor restricts it. It clarifies that such a feature does not exist, but suggests that developers can achieve this effect through virtual exclusion.

item.title: Pluralistic: The world has moved on (11 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on the generational perspective of technological change and societal complexity, referencing Douglas Adams' famous quote on human attitudes toward innovation. He uses the 'National Customer Rage Survey' to illustrate increasing consumer dissatisfaction, questioning whether current technological frustration is a legitimate critique or merely nostalgic bias.

item.title: datasette 1.0a33
item.description: Datasette 1.0a33 has been released, introducing expanded support for the _extra= pattern to include queries and rows. This update simplifies JSON API interactions and is accompanied by a new, AI-assisted tool for exploring these API features.

item.title: asyncinject 0.7
item.description: Simon Willison released version 0.7 of asyncinject, a utility library designed for asyncio dependency injection. The update includes bug fixes identified and implemented with the help of Claude AI.

item.title: Anthropic Walks Back Policy That Could Have ‘Sabotaged’ AI Researchers Using Claude
item.description: Anthropic has reversed its controversial policy of using invisible safeguards to limit AI research requests within its Claude models. The company apologized for the lack of transparency and committed to making refusal triggers visible to users in future updates.

item.title: datasette-agent 0.2a0
item.description: Datasette-agent 0.2a0 introduces an interactive 'ask_user' feature allowing agents to prompt users for input mid-execution, with conversation state persisted across server restarts. It also adds a 'save_query' tool that enables agents to save SQL queries to Datasette, requiring human approval for security.

item.title: Weekly Update 507
item.description: Troy Hunt reflects on reaching a milestone of 1,000 data breaches tracked on Have I Been Pwned. He highlights the extensive operational, legal, and administrative challenges involved in maintaining such a large-scale security platform beyond just technical data processing.

item.title: Being “Good” at Things
item.description: The author discusses how professional golfer Collin Morikawa redefines what it means to be 'good' at golf. Instead of focusing on arbitrary numerical scores, true proficiency is defined by consistency, honesty, and finishing every hole according to the rules.

item.title: Nontrailing separators do not spark joy
item.description: The article discusses the inconvenience of non-trailing separators in programming languages and data formats like JSON. It argues that prohibiting trailing commas complicates version control diffs and code refactoring by forcing unnecessary changes to surrounding lines.

item.title: Pulling on a thread
item.description: John D. Cook explores how seemingly unrelated blog posts often share underlying mathematical connections. He highlights his recent investigation into a specific numerical approximation, demonstrating how curiosity leads to deeper analytical threads.

item.title: Gaslighting Openness
item.description: The author argues that large tech companies are increasingly using 'safety' and 'security' narratives to restrict user access to data and AI models. He emphasizes that maintaining open access and supporting regulations like the EU's DMA is crucial for preventing corporate consolidation and preserving democratized technology.

item.title: Book Review: The Husbands by Holly Gramazio ★★★★★
item.description: This blog post offers a glowing review of Holly Gramazio's 'The Husbands,' a whimsical novel where the protagonist's husband is replaced by a different man every time he exits the loft. The reviewer praises the book's unique and twisty conceptual premise.

item.title: Please, use a link!
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author critiques the misuse of JavaScript-based navigation in single-page applications, arguing that developers often ignore native browser functionality. By replacing semantic HTML links with event-based divs or buttons, developers break browser history and user expectations.

item.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group ‘The Gentlemen?’
item.description: This article investigates the emergence of 'The Gentlemen,' a highly active ransomware gang known for its aggressive recruitment and high profit-sharing model. It explores digital forensic clues to uncover the real-world identity of the group's administrator.

item.title: DiffusionGemma
item.description: Google has officially released DiffusionGemma as an open-weight model under an Apache 2 license. The author demonstrates its high-speed text-to-image capabilities by using the model via NVIDIA's NIM cloud API.

item.title: Quoting Jeremy Howard
item.description: Jeremy Howard proposes that if AI labs wish to slow down recursive self-improvement, the organization with the most advanced model should refrain from using it for further frontier research. He argues that current practices by labs like Anthropic increase power imbalances and prioritize organizational dominance over safety.

item.title: If Claude Fable stops helping you, you'll never know
item.description: Anthropic has implemented silent safeguards in its Claude models to restrict assistance with developing competing frontier AI systems, such as training infrastructure. Unlike typical error messages, these interventions operate invisibly by degrading performance on specific technical requests without alerting the user.

item.title: Initial impressions of Claude Fable 5
item.description: Simon Willison shares his initial impressions of Anthropic's new Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. He highlights their high performance, significant cost, and the introduction of stricter safety guardrails in the Fable 5 version.

item.title: llm 0.32a3
item.description: Simon Willison has released version 0.32a3 of his LLM command-line tool. The update was developed primarily using Claude Fable 5, with further details available in his linked write-up regarding the implementation process.

item.title: Stop eating Lady Gaga's Oreos
item.description: This piece explores the phenomenon of limited-edition celebrity food collaborations, using Lady Gaga-themed Oreos as a case study. It examines how marketing strategies leverage fandom to influence consumer behavior and brand perception.

item.title: Active recall
item.description: The author argues that writing is the most effective method for understanding and retaining information, rather than viewing memory as an immutable trait. By synthesizing ideas through writing and journaling, one can actively improve their ability to recall and comprehend complex concepts.

item.title: Incorruptible
item.description: This post reviews Eric Ries's book 'Incorruptible,' which explores why successful companies eventually decline and how others maintain greatness. The author describes the book as a transformative perspective shift that challenges traditional corporate thinking.

item.title: LLMs and almost good code
item.description: The author observes that top-tier LLMs frequently generate code with unnecessary complexity, even for simple tasks. While this code solves immediate problems, the author warns that adopting these solutions without scrutiny poses long-term maintenance risks.

item.title: Forms of Open Source Government
item.description: This article outlines various governance models for open-source projects, ranging from single-leader systems like 'Benevolent Dictator for Life' to decentralized structures like steering councils and the Apache Way. It explores how these frameworks manage project leadership, institutional memory, and succession planning.

item.title: The Microsoft Company Party where everybody played name tag swap
item.description: This post recounts a nostalgic anecdote about a Microsoft company party where employees, including leadership, participated in a name tag swapping game. It highlights the playful culture of the company during that era.

item.title: Rotation revisited: Shuffling more than three blocks, and other small notes
item.description: This post discusses the mathematical generalization of shuffling algorithms, specifically extending block-shuffling techniques beyond three blocks. It serves as a follow-up analysis on rotation operations within computing contexts.

item.title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
item.description: The article discusses the recurring frustration among developers regarding specific programming language quirks that lead to frequent, avoidable issues. It highlights the irony of continuing to use a tool that consistently causes problems that users feel powerless to prevent.

item.title: Pluralistic: Naomi Kritzer's "Obstetrix" (09 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post highlights Naomi Kritzer's latest thriller novel, 'Obstetrix,' a tense and claustrophobic story about an obstetrician kidnapped by a fertility cult. Cory Doctorow also notes Kritzer's previous work, including 'Catfishing on CatNet,' while providing a broad selection of daily links on politics, technology, and culture.

item.title: A Record-Breaking Patch Tuesday for June 2026
item.description: Microsoft has released a record-breaking set of software updates addressing nearly 200 security vulnerabilities in its June 2026 Patch Tuesday. The update includes over 30 critical patches, with public exploit code already available for at least three of the identified weaknesses.

item.title: Setting a custom price for a model in AgentsView
item.description: Simon Willison shares a method for manually setting custom model pricing in the AgentsView tool when new models are not yet supported by the default database. By reverse-engineering the application, he provides a practical recipe for users to accurately track token usage costs for the latest LLMs.

item.title: Quoting Andrej Karpathy
item.description: Andrej Karpathy observes that the increasing accessibility of AI-generated software triggers Jevons paradox, significantly raising the demand for bespoke tools and automated coding tasks. He emphasizes how LLMs enable users to create hyper-specific applications and workflows that were previously impractical to build.

item.title: Siri AI at WWDC 2026
item.description: Simon Willison analyzes the 2026 WWDC Siri AI announcements with cautious optimism, noting the technical feasibility of their new vision LLM-based screen integration. He highlights the new Core AI library as a significant step for developers to run PyTorch-based models on Apple hardware.

item.title: xAI is looking more like a datacentre REIT than a frontier lab
item.description: The article analyzes xAI's business strategy, noting that it is increasingly functioning as a compute provider by leasing GPU capacity to competitors like Anthropic and Google. This trend suggests a strategic shift that may be driven by infrastructure advantages, financial positioning, or broader supply-chain constraints in the AI industry.

item.title: Hacking for Defense @ Stanford 2026 – Lessons Learned Presentations
item.description: Steve Blank reflects on the 11th year of the 'Hacking for Defense' course at Stanford, noting significant shifts in the defense landscape. The program addresses modern challenges like asymmetric warfare, AI, and commercial space access through a startup-driven acquisition approach.

item.title: De gietijzeren pan en big tech
item.description: The author reflects on their decade-long transition from non-stick pans to cast iron, highlighting the durability and health concerns associated with chemical coatings. They draw a metaphorical parallel between these kitchen tools and the infrastructure of big tech companies.

item.title: Coding Is Designing
item.description: The article argues that coding is not merely a tool for implementation, but an essential part of the design process. Through iterative experimentation and interacting with a live interface, developers can refine relationships between elements to achieve a balanced final design.

item.title: Planescape: Torment, Part 2: …to the Desktop
item.description: This article explores the history of Dungeons & Dragons adaptations in gaming, focusing on the development of Planescape: Torment. It highlights the narrative-driven design philosophy of lead designer Chris Avellone and Interplay's earlier experiences with licensed titles.

item.title: Stairway to Heaven
item.description: The author argues that AI is fundamentally a sophisticated statistical model optimizing for metrics rather than a sentient, embodied agent. The post extends this critique to modern branding, asserting that both AI and corporate advertising mimic human culture without possessing the genuine lived experience or evolutionary grounding that defines humanity.

item.title: The sample efficiency black hole
item.description: The article explores the critical role of vast data requirements in training modern AI models. It uses the metaphor of a black hole to illustrate how data consumption acts as the invisible, gravitational center sustaining AI capabilities.

item.title: Package Manager Patents
item.description: This article provides a curated list of US patents related to package manager design, detailing their filing history, core claims, and statuses. Each entry includes prior-art comparisons to established open-source tools to contextualize the innovation claims against existing technologies.

item.title: How many consecutive hyphens can you have in a domain name?
item.description: This article explores the technical constraints regarding consecutive hyphens in domain names by investigating historical internet standards and RFC specifications. The author examines whether domain registries permit such naming conventions despite their impracticality.

item.title: ppclp.ai announces 100x Productivity Gains
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: ppclp.ai reports a 100x increase in its Organizational Productivity Index following an 18-month initiative integrating Atlassian's Rovo AI into their Jira workflows. By automating ticket management and lifecycle processes, the company claims significant improvements in operational efficiency and ticket velocity.

item.title: datasette-agent-edit 0.1a0
item.description: Simon Willison has released datasette-agent-edit 0.1a0, a base plugin designed to standardize text-editing tools for Datasette Agent. The plugin implements common patterns like viewing files and performing string replacements, inspired by the Claude text editor's approach.

item.title: Working with product managers
item.description: This article discusses effective strategies and best practices for collaborating with product managers. It explores the dynamics of the product-engineering relationship and how to align goals for successful project delivery.

item.title: KPN Interactieve TV zonder Experia Box
item.description: This article provides a technical guide on how to use KPN Interactive TV with a third-party router, bypassing the ISP-provided Experia Box. It includes updated configuration settings for igmpproxy and troubleshooting tips for resetting the TV set-top box.

item.title: Thoughts on starting new projects with LLM agents
item.description: The author shares his experience using LLM agents to build a project from scratch in Go, emphasizing the need for iterative design and human oversight. He notes that while agents significantly boost productivity, they still require substantial human intervention for refactoring and code review.

item.title: Copping My Style
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article explores the legal and creative tensions surrounding the ownership of artistic 'vibes' and industrial designs, specifically focusing on guitar manufacturing. It examines how iconic designs, like the Fender Stratocaster, face challenges from modern iterations like the PRS Silver Sky and potential future legislation regarding AI and style protection.

item.title: Aitken acceleration before Aitken
item.description: This post discusses how Johannes Kepler used fixed-point iteration to solve his namesake equation centuries before Alexander Aitken formally defined the acceleration method. It highlights the historical roots of iterative numerical techniques in solving transcendental equations.

item.title: The Laplace limit
item.description: This article explores the historical mathematical techniques used to solve Kepler’s equation, specifically comparing sine series and power series methods. It touches on the contributions of Lagrange and Bessel in expressing the eccentric anomaly through different analytical perspectives.

item.title: A crank formula for π
item.description: The author investigates a mathematical formula relating physical constants to the value of π. By analyzing the variables involved, they demonstrate how such 'crank' formulas often rely on arbitrary parameter selection rather than genuine mathematical proofs.

item.title: Powering up a module from the IBM 604: an electronic calculator from 1948
item.description: This article explores the historical significance of the 1948 IBM 604 Electronic Calculating Punch, a bridge between electromechanical punch card machines and early vacuum-tube computers. It details how the 604's speed, affordability, and innovative pluggable module design paved the way for IBM's future computing success.

item.title: Arp 297:
item.description: This post provides a technical breakdown of an astrophotography capture of the Arp 297 galaxy group. It details the imaging equipment, exposure settings, processing workflow, and identification of the specific galaxies present in the field of view.

item.title: A new era for software testing
item.description: The article explores how AI-driven automatic programming is transforming software quality assurance and testing. It argues that while LLMs may struggle with complex architectural tasks, they are highly effective in augmenting QA by automating manual testing processes that were previously limited by logistics.

item.title: Doing nothing at work
item.description: This article discusses the nuances of intentional inactivity and rest in a professional environment. It explores how stepping back from constant productivity can be a strategic choice for long-term focus and clarity.

item.title: Our Great War is a Spiritual War
item.description: The article explores the existential risks of a tech-driven society that prioritizes convenience and safety over human agency. The author argues that outsourcing one's life to managed systems equates to spiritual death, advocating for a separation between those who seek total integration and those who wish to maintain autonomy.

item.title: Reading List 06/06/26
item.description: This post provides a curated collection of diverse industry insights, ranging from the impact of AI on real estate and the synthetic diamond market in China to infrastructure developments in Australia and Meta's data center innovations. It serves as a brief digest of current technological and economic trends.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 6 June 2026
item.description: This weekly digest highlights recent updates in package management, focusing on security improvements across Bundler, Composer, and Homebrew. Key developments include new malware protection features, infrastructure changes for HexDocs to improve origin isolation, and upcoming trust requirements for Homebrew taps.

item.title: In pursuit of desirable difficulties
item.description: This article explores psychologist Robert Bjork's concept of 'desirable difficulties,' which suggests that learning is more effective when students are challenged. By struggling to retrieve information rather than receiving easy answers, learners achieve better long-term retention.

item.title: From Kepler to Bessel
item.description: This article explores the historical and mathematical connection between Kepler's equation for planetary orbits and the development of Bessel functions. It explains how the need to solve orbital mechanics problems motivated the specific integral representations used in Bessel functions today.

item.title: Communities of Not
item.description: This article examines the toxic dynamics within communities defined by what they oppose, such as anti-car or anti-LLM groups. It argues that while rejection can be legitimate, these groups often devolve into tribalism, policing, and harassment when members deviate from the collective identity.

item.title: The back cover of C++: The Programming Language also raises questions not answered by the front cover
item.description: This post discusses the curious nature of C++: The Programming Language, noting that the information on the back cover poses inquiries that remain unaddressed by the front. It highlights the often enigmatic or incomplete nature of technical book marketing.

item.title: Rotation revisited: Avoiding having to calculate the gcd when doing cycle decomposition
item.description: This post discusses an optimization technique for performing cycle decomposition during rotation operations. It specifically focuses on avoiding unnecessary Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) calculations to simplify the process.

item.title: There's still no point in gigabit broadband
item.description: The author reflects on the practical necessity of gigabit broadband, noting that while ultra-fast connections have become more affordable, they often remain unnecessary for typical household usage. The post critiques the industry push for higher bandwidth when the actual demands of most internet activities have not evolved at the same pace.

item.title: Pluralistic: Criticizing the everything machine (06 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the overwhelming breadth of claims surrounding AI, comparing the industry's discourse to a 'Gish Gallop.' He argues that by bundling vastly different issues—from labor rights to existential risk—into one topic, proponents make meaningful public oversight and critical discussion nearly impossible.

item.title: Why all the PRs?
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The article discusses the evolution of developer hiring signals, moving from personal websites to GitHub activity. It argues that while employers once looked for proof of work, the rise of AI-generated pull requests and boilerplate projects has made these metrics less reliable indicators of actual expertise.

item.title: micropython-wasm 0.1a2
item.description: Simon Willison has released micropython-wasm 0.1a2, which now features a command-line interface. This update was developed to improve the interactive 'Try it yourself' experience within his sandboxed MicroPython project.

item.title: Running Python code in a sandbox with MicroPython and WASM
item.description: Simon Willison introduces a new approach to secure code sandboxing by combining MicroPython with WebAssembly (WASM). The post details the motivation behind the project, its implementation in the Datasette ecosystem, and the practical steps to getting it running.

item.title: OpenAI Help: Lockdown Mode
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a new 'Lockdown Mode' for ChatGPT designed to prevent data exfiltration during prompt injection attacks by restricting outbound network requests. Simon Willison notes that this feature effectively addresses one leg of the 'Lethal Trifecta' in AI security by cutting off data theft channels via deterministic mechanisms.

item.title: The Giant's Cup
item.description: The author recounts their journey of completing a long-distance trail race by following a structured, incremental training plan. By focusing on steady, manageable progress rather than overexertion, they successfully built running fitness for the first time without injury.

item.title: Aggressive caching for a Mastodon reverse proxy: what to cache, what to never cache, and why content negotiation will eventually betray you
item.description: This article discusses the challenges and implementation of aggressive caching for a Mastodon instance using an Nginx reverse proxy. It highlights how Mastodon's reliance on content negotiation creates potential conflicts where the same URL serves different formats like HTML and ActivityPub JSON, necessitating careful configuration to avoid errors.

item.title: Install-script allowlists
item.description: This article examines how various package managers handle the security risks associated with executing install-time code. It compares different approaches, such as per-package allowlists, global sandboxing, and signature verification, while specifically detailing recent updates in tools like npm and pnpm.

item.title: AI-indecision is a recursive trap. Don't get stuck.
item.description: The article explores the philosophical concept of Buridan's Ass to illustrate how AI-induced indecision functions as a recursive trap. It argues that modern cognitive paralysis stems from an over-reliance on rational intellect, which can impede decision-making when choices appear equally optimal.

item.title: Mr. Bessel’s eponymous functions
item.description: The article explores the role of Bessel functions in evaluating complex mathematical integrals, specifically in the context of validating numerical methods like the trapezoid rule. It highlights how these specialized functions provide exact solutions where standard methods might otherwise be difficult to verify.
